## Our path today

<div style="font-size: 1em; line-height: 2; text-align: center;">
Random variables, distributions, and moments<br>
&darr;<br>
Regression: scalar and matrix OLS<br>
&darr;<br>
Hypothesis testing: from a fair coin to an OLS slope
</div>

::: fragment
By the end, you should be able to **read a probability distribution,
summarize uncertainty, and understand how OLS estimates a regression**.
:::

::: notes
Introduce the two-part path. Emphasize that distributions prepare the
language needed for regression.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), Chapters 1-4; the regression section is an
instructor-developed introduction to least squares.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Learning objectives

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

1.  distinguish discrete and continuous random variables;
2.  read a PMF and a PDF and draw a histogram;
3.  calculate Uniform and Normal interval probabilities;
4.  transform and standardize a Normal variable;
5.  compute expectation, variance, covariance, and correlation;
6.  derive and calculate simple OLS estimates with and without an intercept;
7.  write multiple regression in matrix form and calculate the OLS estimate;
8.  explain how a low-probability observation can challenge a null hypothesis;
9.  state the hypotheses in an OLS slope $t$-test and interpret its two tails.

::: notes
The regression goal is estimation: first with scalar algebra, then with
matrix algebra.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), Chapters 1-4.
:::

# 1. Random variables, distributions, and moments

## A random variable turns outcomes into numbers

A random variable is a rule

$$
X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R.
$$

Example: toss a coin twice and let $X$ be the number of heads.

$$
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{Outcome} & TT & HT & TH & HH\\ \hline
X & 0 & 1 & 1 & 2
\end{array}
$$

::: notes
Explain that the outcome can be a word or a sequence, while the random
variable assigns it a numerical value that we can analyze.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 22-24.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Discrete example 1: the number of heads has a PMF

For the number of heads in two fair tosses:

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2\\ \hline
P(X=x) & 1/4 & 1/2 & 1/4
\end{array}
$$

The probabilities must satisfy

$$
p_X(x)\ge0,
\qquad
\sum_xp_X(x)=1.
$$

::: notes
This table is the **probability mass function (PMF)**. Link each
probability back to the four equally likely coin outcomes.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 22-25.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Discrete example 2: Bernoulli

A Bernoulli random variable records success as 1 and failure as 0:

$$
X=\begin{cases}
1, & \text{success},\\
0, & \text{failure}.
\end{cases}
$$

If $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, then

$$
p_X(1)=p,
\qquad
p_X(0)=1-p.
$$

Example: $X=1$ if a student passes and $X=0$ otherwise.

::: notes
This is the simplest discrete distribution. Emphasize that the PMF gives
a probability to each possible value.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), p. 56.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 1: read a PMF {.compact-exercise}

Let $X$ be the number of heads in two fair tosses:

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2\\ \hline
p_X(x) & 1/4 & 1/2 & 1/4
\end{array}
$$

Find:

1.  $P(X=1)$;
2.  $P(X\ge1)$;
3.  $P(X\le1)$.

::: notes
$P(X=1)=1/2$.
$P(X\ge1)=P(X=1)+P(X=2)=3/4$.
$P(X\le1)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)=3/4$.

\[Sources\] - Exercise constructed from Hansen (2021), pp. 22-31.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: draw a histogram from frequencies {.compact-example}

::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
The sample is

<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.7;">
$4,\ 12,\ 15,\ 18,\ 22,$<br>
$24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 31,\ 36.$
</div>

Group the observations into intervals of width 10:

| Interval | Frequency |
|:---------|----------:|
| $[0,10)$ | 1 |
| $[10,20)$ | 3 |
| $[20,30)$ | 4 |
| $[30,40)$ | 2 |
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Draw it by hand:

1. put the intervals on the horizontal axis;
2. use frequency as the height;
3. draw touching rectangles.
:::
:::

::: notes
Read the sample one value at a time and place each value in an interval.
Then draw the axes, mark the four interval boundaries, and draw one
rectangle at a time. The rectangles touch because the intervals represent
adjacent ranges of a numerical variable.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed data.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example solution: the rectangles touch

```{r}
#| label: plot-histogram-example
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: "88%"
hist_values <- c(4, 12, 15, 18, 22, 24, 25, 27, 31, 36)
hist(hist_values, breaks = seq(0, 40, 10), right = FALSE,
     col = adjustcolor("#2E86C1", 0.55), border = "white",
     main = "Histogram from a frequency table",
     xlab = "Interval", ylab = "Frequency", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 40, 10))
```

::: notes
Check that the four heights are 1, 3, 4, and 2. The total frequency is 10.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed data and R figure.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 2: draw a histogram {.compact-exercise}

Use the **same sample** from the example:

$$
4,\ 12,\ 15,\ 18,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 31,\ 36.
$$

Now use the narrower intervals below:

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$$
[0,5),\ [5,10),\ [10,15),\ [15,20)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$
[20,25),\ [25,30),\ [30,35),\ [35,40)
$$
:::
:::

1. Count the frequency in each interval.
2. Draw the histogram using frequency as the height.
3. Compare it with the histogram from the example.

::: notes
The frequencies are $1,0,1,2,2,2,1,1$. The bars should touch. The two
histograms use exactly the same observations; only the interval width has
changed. Narrower intervals show more detail, but each bar is based on
fewer observations.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Discrete variables use a PMF; continuous variables use a PDF

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Discrete random variable**

Takes separated values.

Examples: number of heads, number of children.

Use a **probability mass function (PMF)**:

$$
p_X(x)=P(X=x).
$$

$$
p_X(x)\ge0,
\quad
\sum_xp_X(x)=1.
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Continuous random variable**

Can take any value in an interval.

Examples: height, time, income.

Use a **probability density function (PDF)**:

$$
f_X(x)\ge0.
$$

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(x)\,dx=1.
$$
:::
:::

::: notes
Do not develop integrals on this slide. The main distinction is separated
values versus a continuum of values.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 22-39.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## For a PDF, area represents probability

For a continuous random variable,

$$
\boxed{P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx}.
$$

The probability is the **area under the PDF** between $a$ and $b$.

At one exact value, there is no width and therefore no area:

$$P(X=x)=0.$$

::: notes
Say: the vertical height is density, but the area is probability. A tall
curve at one point does not itself give a probability. Probability needs
an interval with positive width.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 29-39.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The shaded area is an interval probability

```{r}
#| label: plot-density-area
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: "88%"
x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 600)
y <- dnorm(x)
plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#154360",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density", ylim = c(0, 0.43),
     main = "Probability is the area under the density")
xs <- x[x >= -1 & x <= 1]
polygon(c(-1, xs, 1), c(0, dnorm(xs), 0),
        col = adjustcolor("#2E86C1", alpha.f = 0.35), border = NA)
lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = "#154360")
abline(v = c(-1, 1), lty = 3, col = "#777777")
text(0, 0.12, expression(P(-1 <= X~and~X <= 1)), col = "#154360")
```

::: notes
Explain that the height of the curve is density, not probability at one
exact point. Probability over an interval is the shaded area.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 29-39; figure generated in R.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Uniform PDF has constant height

If $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)$, then

$$
f_X(x)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a},&a\le x\le b,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The height is $1/(b-a)$ so that the total rectangular area is

$$
(b-a)\frac{1}{b-a}=1.
$$

::: notes
Draw the rectangular PDF. Its width is $b-a$, so its height must be
$1/(b-a)$ for the total area to equal one.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 36-39.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: calculate a Uniform probability {.compact-example}

Suppose

$$X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,10).$$

Find $P(2\le X\le5)$.

The PDF height is

$$\frac{1}{10-0}=0.1.$$

Therefore,

$$
P(2\le X\le5)
=(5-2)(0.1)
=0.3.
$$

::: notes
Probability is the rectangular area: interval width 3 times PDF height
0.1. Also point out that $P(X=2)=0$ even though $f_X(2)=0.1$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example based on Hansen (2021),
pp. 36-39.
:::

## Continuous example 2: Normal

Write $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\mu$ sets the center and $\sigma$
sets the spread.

```{r}
#| label: plot-normal-distributions
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "78%"
x <- seq(-6, 8, length.out = 700)
plot(x, dnorm(x, 0, 1), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#154360",
     ylim = c(0, 0.43), xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Normal distributions: mean sets location, variance sets spread")
lines(x, dnorm(x, 2, 1), lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B", lty = 2)
lines(x, dnorm(x, 0, 2), lwd = 3, col = "#1E8449", lty = 3)
legend("topright",
       c("N(0, 1)", "N(2, 1)", "N(0, 4)"),
       col = c("#154360", "#C0392B", "#1E8449"),
       lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2, 3), bty = "n")
```

::: notes
The red curve moves the mean from zero to two without changing the
variance. The green curve keeps mean zero but increases the variance
from one to four, making the distribution more spread out.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 61, 113-116; figure generated in R.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Linear transformations of a Normal variable stay Normal

Suppose

$$X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).$$

For constants $a$ and $b$,

$$
\boxed{a+bX\sim N\!\left(a+b\mu,\;b^2\sigma^2\right)}.
$$

Important special cases:

$$
X+a\sim N(\mu+a,\sigma^2),
\qquad
bX\sim N(b\mu,b^2\sigma^2).
$$

::: notes
Adding a constant moves the center but does not change the variance.
Multiplying by $b$ multiplies the mean by $b$ and the variance by $b^2$.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 61, 113-116.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Standardization is a Normal transformation

If


$$X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),$$

subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation:

$$
\boxed{Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)}.
$$

The standardized value tells us how many standard deviations $X$ is above
or below its mean.

::: notes
Connect this directly to the preceding transformation formula by taking
$a=-\mu/\sigma$ and $b=1/\sigma$.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 113-116.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: a Normal interval after standardizing {.compact-example}

Exam scores satisfy

$$X\sim N(70,10^2).$$

Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and suppose you are given

$$P(-1\le Z\le1)=0.6827.$$

Find $P(60\le X\le80)$.

::: notes
Pause here and ask students what transformation would turn $X$ into a
standard Normal variable.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example solution: standardize both endpoints {.compact-example}

Standardize both endpoints:

$$
\frac{60-70}{10}=-1,
\qquad
\frac{80-70}{10}=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(60\le X\le80)
&=P(-1\le Z\le1)\\
&=0.6827.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: notes
First identify the mean and standard deviation. Standardize each endpoint,
then use the standard-Normal probability supplied in the question.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 3A: Uniform probability {.compact-exercise}

Suppose

$$X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(2,8).$$

1. Plot the PDF.
2. Calculate $P(3\le X\le6)$.

::: notes
The PDF height is $1/(8-2)=1/6$.
The interval has width $6-3=3$, so

$$
P(3\le X\le6)=3\left(\frac16\right)=\frac12.
$$

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 3B: transform a Normal variable {.compact-exercise}

Suppose

$$X\sim N(50,5^2),
\qquad
Y=2X+10.
$$

Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and suppose

$$P(-1\le Z\le1)=0.6827.$$

1. Find the distributions of $X+10$, $2X$, and $Y$.
2. Calculate $P(100\le Y\le120)$.

::: notes
$X+10\sim N(60,5^2)$, $2X\sim N(100,10^2)$, and
$Y\sim N(110,10^2)$. For the interval,

$$
\frac{100-110}{10}=-1,
\qquad
\frac{120-110}{10}=1.
$$

Therefore $P(100\le Y\le120)=P(-1\le Z\le1)=0.6827$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Expectation is a probability-weighted average

For a discrete random variable,

$$
E(X)=\sum_x xP(X=x).
$$

::: fragment
Expectation is the long-run average value across many repetitions.
:::

::: fragment
It does not need to be one of the values that $X$ can actually take.
:::

::: notes
Distinguish the expected value from the most likely value. It is a center
of the distribution, formed by weighting each value by its probability.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 25-28, 37-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: expected number of heads

For two fair tosses,

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2\\ \hline
P(X=x) & 1/4 & 1/2 & 1/4
\end{array}
$$

::: fragment
$$
\begin{aligned}
E(X)
&=0\left(\frac14\right)
+1\left(\frac12\right)
+2\left(\frac14\right)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: notes
Read the calculation aloud as “value times probability, then add.”

\[Sources\] - Example constructed from Hansen (2021), pp. 25-28.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 4: calculate an expectation {.compact-exercise}

A simple investment has payoff $X$:

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
x & -2 & 0 & 4\\ \hline
P(X=x) & 0.25 & 0.50 & 0.25
\end{array}
$$

1.  Verify that the probabilities sum to one.
2.  Find $E(X)$.
3.  Is the expected payoff equal to the most likely payoff?

::: notes
The probabilities sum to $0.25+0.50+0.25=1$.
$E(X)=(-2)(0.25)+(0)(0.50)+(4)(0.25)=0.5$.
The most likely payoff is 0, while the expected payoff is 0.5. The
expected value does not need to be a value that $X$ can take.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise based on Hansen (2021),
pp. 25-28.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Expectation is linear

For constants $a$ and $b$,

$$
E(a+bX)=a+bE(X).
$$

::: fragment
For two random variables,

$$
E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y),
$$

whether or not $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
:::

::: fragment
In general, $E[g(X)]\ne g(E[X])$.
:::

::: notes
Use a wage conversion example: if annual earnings equal 12 times monthly
earnings, expected annual earnings equal 12 times expected monthly
earnings.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 25-28, 40-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Variance measures spread around the mean

Let $\mu=E(X)$. Then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2].
$$

::: fragment
An equivalent formula is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2.
$$
:::

::: fragment
The standard deviation is

$$
\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
$$
:::

::: notes
Variance is an average squared distance from the mean. Squaring prevents
positive and negative deviations from cancelling. Standard deviation is
in the original units.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 40-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: variance of the number of heads

We already found $E(X)=1$.

::: fragment
$$
E(X^2)
=0^2\left(\frac14\right)
+1^2\left(\frac12\right)
+2^2\left(\frac14\right)
=\frac32.
$$
:::

::: fragment
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2
=\frac32-1^2
=\frac12.
$$
:::

::: notes
Keep the distinction between $E(X^2)$ and $[E(X)]^2$ visible.

\[Sources\] - Example constructed from Hansen (2021), pp. 40-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 5: expectation and variance {.compact-exercise}

Use the investment payoff:

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
x & -2 & 0 & 4\\ \hline
P(X=x) & 0.25 & 0.50 & 0.25
\end{array}
$$

Given $E(X)=0.5$:

1.  calculate $E(X^2)$;
2.  calculate $\operatorname{Var}(X)$;
3.  calculate $\operatorname{SD}(X)$.

::: notes
$E(X^2)=4(0.25)+0(0.50)+16(0.25)=5$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X)=5-(0.5)^2=4.75$.
$\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{4.75}\approx2.179$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise based on Hansen (2021),
pp. 40-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A shift changes the mean but not the variance

For constants $a$ and $b$,

$$
E(a+bX)=a+bE(X),
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}(a+bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X).
$$

::: fragment
Adding $a$ shifts every value equally, so spread does not change.
:::

::: fragment
Multiplying by $b$ changes every distance from the mean by $|b|$.
:::

::: notes
Contrast the two effects. A location shift changes the center; a scale
change affects both center and spread.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 40-42.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Covariance describes how two variables move together

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=E[(X-E(X))(Y-E(Y))].
$$

::: fragment
Equivalently,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y).
$$
:::

::: fragment
Positive: they tend to move in the same direction.  
Negative: they tend to move in opposite directions.
:::

::: notes
Say that covariance combines two deviations. When both deviations have
the same sign, their product is positive.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 91-93.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Correlation puts covariance on a common scale

$$
\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}
{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)}.
$$

::: fragment
$$-1\le\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)\le1.$$
:::

::: fragment
Correlation measures the direction and strength of a **linear**
relationship.
:::

::: notes
Covariance depends on units; correlation does not. Zero correlation does
not rule out a nonlinear relationship.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 91-94.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Correlation changes the shape of a scatter plot

```{r}
#| label: plot-correlation-patterns
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| out-width: "96%"
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1))
n <- 80
x <- rnorm(n)
y_pos <- 0.8*x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.45)
y_zero <- rnorm(n)
y_neg <- -0.8*x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.45)
plot(x, y_pos, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#2E86C1", 0.65),
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", main = "Positive")
plot(x, y_zero, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#7F8C8D", 0.65),
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", main = "Near zero")
plot(x, y_neg, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#C0392B", 0.65),
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", main = "Negative")
par(oldpar)
```

::: notes
Ask students to describe direction before naming correlation. The middle
panel has no clear linear direction.

\[Sources\] - Hansen (2021), pp. 91-94; simulated figures generated in R.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 6: covariance and correlation {.compact-exercise}

Three equally likely observations are

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
&1&2&3\\ \hline
X&1&2&3\\
Y&1&3&2
\end{array}
$$

Treat each column as having probability $1/3$.

1.  Find $E(X)$ and $E(Y)$.
2.  Find $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$.
3.  Find $\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)$.

::: notes
$E(X)=E(Y)=2$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=[(-1)(-1)+0(1)+(1)(0)]/3=1/3$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2/3$.
Therefore $\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=(1/3)/(2/3)=1/2$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise based on Hansen (2021),
pp. 91-94.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Regression: estimating a line

## What is regression?

Regression uses a line to summarize how an outcome $Y$ changes with an
explanatory variable $X$:

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+u_i.
$$

::: fragment
- $\beta_0$: intercept;
- $\beta_1$: slope;
- $u_i$: the part of $Y_i$ not described by the line.
:::

::: fragment
From data, we estimate the line

$$
\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_i.
$$
:::

::: notes
Say: “Regression draws one line through a cloud of points. The line cannot
usually pass through every point, so we need a rule for choosing the best
line. That rule will be ordinary least squares.”

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed introduction to linear regression.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Which line is best? What rule should decide?

```{r}
#| label: plot-three-candidate-lines
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| out-width: "88%"
hours <- c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 4.5, 5, 6, 6.5, 7.5, 8)
score <- c(53, 55, 54, 58, 59, 61, 63, 64, 68, 69, 73, 75)
candidate_a <- lm(score ~ hours)
plot(hours, score, pch = 19, cex = 1.35, col = "#2E86C1",
     xlab = "Study hours (X)", ylab = "Exam score (Y)",
     xlim = c(0.5, 8.5), ylim = c(48, 79),
     main = "Three candidate lines")
abline(candidate_a, lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B")
abline(a = 55, b = 1.8, lwd = 3, col = "#1E8449", lty = 2)
abline(a = 44, b = 4.2, lwd = 3, col = "#8E44AD", lty = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Observed scores", "Line A", "Line B", "Line C"),
       col = c("#2E86C1", "#C0392B", "#1E8449", "#8E44AD"),
       pch = c(19, NA, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 1, 2, 3),
       lwd = c(NA, 3, 3, 3), bty = "n")
```

::: notes
Ask students to vote for Line A, B, or C. Do not reveal the answer yet.
Then ask what “best” should mean. Visual judgment is not enough when many
lines look plausible. The next slide introduces a numerical rule that can
compare every possible line.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed data and R figure.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ordinary Least Squares minimizes squared residuals

For a candidate line $b_0+b_1X_i$, the residual is

$$
e_i=Y_i-(b_0+b_1X_i).
$$

::: fragment
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) chooses $b_0$ and $b_1$ to minimize

$$
S(b_0,b_1)
=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i\right]^2.
$$
:::

::: fragment
Why square the residuals? Positive and negative errors cannot cancel, and
large errors receive more weight.
:::

::: notes
Say: “Every possible line produces residuals. We square them, add them,
and choose the line with the smallest total.” Connect this directly to
unconstrained minimization from calculus.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed OLS explanation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 1: differentiate the OLS objective

The two first-order conditions are

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial b_0}
=-2\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i)=0,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial b_1}
=-2\sum_{i=1}^nX_i(Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i)=0.
$$

::: fragment
The first condition gives

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\overline Y-\widehat\beta_1\overline X.
$$
:::

::: notes
Differentiate one squared residual on the board first. For the intercept,
the inner derivative is $-1$; for the slope, it is $-X_i$. Divide the
first condition by $n$ to obtain the intercept formula.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed scalar OLS derivation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2: solve for the slope and intercept

Substitute $\widehat\beta_0=\overline Y-\widehat\beta_1\overline X$ into
the second first-order condition:

$$
\boxed{
\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)(Y_i-\overline Y)}
{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline X)^2}}
$$

::: fragment
Then calculate

$$
\boxed{\widehat\beta_0
=\overline Y-\widehat\beta_1\overline X}.
$$
:::

::: fragment
The fitted regression line is
$\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_i$.
:::

::: notes
Say: “The slope compares how X and Y move together with how much X moves
by itself. Once we know the slope, the intercept makes the fitted line pass
through $(\overline X,\overline Y)$.”

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed scalar OLS derivation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: study hours and exam scores {.compact-example}

Suppose we observe four students:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
i&1&2&3&4\\ \hline
X_i\text{ (hours)}&1&2&3&4\\
Y_i\text{ (score)}&52&53&55&56
\end{array}
$$

Calculate the OLS slope and intercept.

::: fragment
First,

$$
\overline X=2.5,
\qquad
\overline Y=54.
$$
:::

::: notes
Reveal only the means after students have calculated them. Then build the
deviation table on the next slide.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example and data.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example solution: plug the data into the formulas {.compact-example}

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr|rr|rr}
i&X_i&Y_i&X_i-\bar X&Y_i-\bar Y&
(X_i-\bar X)(Y_i-\bar Y)&(X_i-\bar X)^2\\ \hline
1&1&52&-1.5&-2&3&2.25\\
2&2&53&-0.5&-1&0.5&0.25\\
3&3&55&0.5&1&0.5&0.25\\
4&4&56&1.5&2&3&2.25\\ \hline
&&&&&7&5
\end{array}
$$

::: fragment
$$
\widehat\beta_1=\frac75=1.4,
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=54-(1.4)(2.5)=50.5.
$$

$$
\boxed{\widehat Y=50.5+1.4X}
$$
:::

::: notes
Interpret the slope: one additional study hour is associated with a 1.4
point increase in the fitted exam score. At two hours, the fitted score is
$50.5+1.4(2)=53.3$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 7: OLS without an intercept {.compact-exercise}

Suppose the fitted line is forced through the origin:

$$
Y_i=\beta X_i+u_i.
$$

1. Starting from
   $S(b)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-bX_i)^2$, differentiate with respect to $b$ and
   show that

   $$\widehat\beta=\frac{\sum_iX_iY_i}{\sum_iX_i^2}.$$

2. Use $X=(1,2,3)$ and $Y=(2,3,5)$ to calculate $\widehat\beta$ and write
   the fitted line.

::: notes
Differentiate:
$dS/db=-2\sum_iX_i(Y_i-bX_i)=0$.
Therefore $\widehat\beta=\sum_iX_iY_i/\sum_iX_i^2$.
For the data, $\sum_iX_iY_i=2+6+15=23$ and
$\sum_iX_i^2=1+4+9=14$. Hence
$\widehat\beta=23/14\approx1.643$ and
$\widehat Y=(23/14)X$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Multiple regression uses matrices

With several explanatory variables,

$$
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf u.
$$

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
$$
\mathbf y=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n
\end{bmatrix}_{n\times1},
\qquad
\mathbf u=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1\\u_2\\\vdots\\u_n
\end{bmatrix}_{n\times1}.
$$

Each row is one observation.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
$$
\boldsymbol\beta=
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_{k-1}
\end{bmatrix}_{k\times1}.
$$

Each entry is one coefficient.
:::
:::

::: notes
Start with dimensions. The outcome vector and error vector contain one
number for each observation. The coefficient vector contains one number
for each column of the design matrix.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed matrix notation for multiple regression.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The design matrix contains the explanatory variables

$$
\mathbf X=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&X_{11}&X_{12}&\cdots&X_{1,k-1}\\
1&X_{21}&X_{22}&\cdots&X_{2,k-1}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
1&X_{n1}&X_{n2}&\cdots&X_{n,k-1}
\end{bmatrix}_{n\times k}.
$$

::: fragment
- one **row** for each observation;
- one **column** for each coefficient;
- the first column of ones produces the intercept $\beta_0$.
:::

::: fragment
For observation $i$, the matrix equation reproduces

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_{k-1}X_{i,k-1}+u_i.
$$
:::

::: notes
Point across one row of X and then down the coefficient vector. Their dot
product gives the fitted value for that observation.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed matrix notation for multiple regression.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Matrix OLS: write and expand the objective {.compact-example}

::: columns
::: {.column width="67%"}
OLS minimizes

$$
S(\mathbf b)
=(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)'
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b).
$$

Expand the product:

$$
S(\mathbf b)
=\mathbf y'\mathbf y
-2\mathbf b'\mathbf X'\mathbf y
+\mathbf b'\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b.
$$
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
<div style="border: 2px solid #777; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.55em; font-size: 0.78em;">
<strong>Matrix derivative rules</strong>

$$
\frac{\partial(\mathbf b'\mathbf c)}{\partial\mathbf b}
=\mathbf c
$$

$$
\frac{\partial(\mathbf b'\mathbf A\mathbf b)}
{\partial\mathbf b}
=(\mathbf A+\mathbf A')\mathbf b
$$

If $\mathbf A$ is symmetric, this is $2\mathbf A\mathbf b$.
</div>
:::
:::

::: notes
The objective is still the sum of squared residuals. Matrix notation only
allows all residuals and all coefficients to be handled at once. In the
quadratic term, $X'X$ is symmetric.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed matrix OLS derivation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Matrix OLS: differentiate and solve {.compact-example}

::: columns
::: {.column width="67%"}
Differentiate:

$$
\frac{\partial S(\mathbf b)}{\partial\mathbf b}
=-2\mathbf X'\mathbf y
+2\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b.
$$

Set the derivative equal to zero:

$$
\mathbf X'\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X'\mathbf y.
$$

If $\mathbf X'\mathbf X$ is invertible,

$$
\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y}.
$$
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
<div style="border: 2px solid #777; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.55em; font-size: 0.78em;">
<strong>Rules used</strong>

$$
\frac{\partial(\mathbf y'\mathbf y)}{\partial\mathbf b}=\mathbf0
$$

$$
\frac{\partial(-2\mathbf b'\mathbf X'\mathbf y)}
{\partial\mathbf b}=-2\mathbf X'\mathbf y
$$

$$
\frac{\partial(\mathbf b'\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b)}
{\partial\mathbf b}=2\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b
$$
</div>
:::
:::

::: notes
Say: “This is the same three-step process as before: write the squared
error, differentiate, and solve. The matrix inverse solves all first-order
conditions simultaneously.”

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed matrix OLS derivation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 8: calculate matrix OLS {.compact-exercise}

Let

$$
\mathbf X=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
1&2\\
1&3
\end{bmatrix}_{3\times2},
\qquad
\mathbf y=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\3\\5
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf X'=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1&1\\
1&2&3
\end{bmatrix}_{2\times3}.
$$

1. Calculate $\mathbf X'\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf X'\mathbf y$.

::: fragment
For Step 2, use

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
3&6\\
6&14
\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
=\frac16
\begin{bmatrix}
14&-6\\
-6&3
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

2. Use this inverse to calculate
   $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y$.
3. Write the fitted regression line.
:::

::: notes
$X'X=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{bmatrix}$ and
$X'y=\begin{bmatrix}10\\23\end{bmatrix}$.
The inverse is
$(X'X)^{-1}=\frac16\begin{bmatrix}14&-6\\-6&3\end{bmatrix}$.
Therefore
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\begin{bmatrix}1/3\\3/2\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\widehat Y=1/3+(3/2)X$.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed exercise.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. Hypothesis testing

## Is this coin-tossing game fair?

We play the following game:

- if heads appears more often, **I win**;
- if tails appears more often, **you win**.

::: fragment
If the coin is fair, both of us should have the same chance of winning.
:::

::: fragment
We toss the coin 50 times and observe

$$
\boxed{48\text{ heads and }2\text{ tails}.}
$$

Does the coin still look fair?
:::

::: notes
Ask for an immediate reaction before showing any formula. Most students
will say that 48 heads feels too unusual for a fair coin. The next slide
turns that reaction into mathematical language.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed hypothesis-testing example.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The null hypothesis gives us a reference distribution

Start by temporarily assuming that the coin is fair:

$$
H_0:p=0.5.
$$

::: fragment
Under $H_0$, $X$ counts successes in 50 independent
$\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5)$ trials, so

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(50,0.5).
$$
:::

::: fragment
If $H_0$ is true, values near 25 heads are common. Values near 0 or 50
heads are rare.
:::

::: notes
Say: “We did not begin by proving that the coin is fair. We temporarily
assumed fairness. This assumption gives us a reference distribution. We
can now ask whether the observed result is normal or surprising under that
distribution.”

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example using the Binomial distribution.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A very small tail probability makes us doubt $H_0$

We observed $X=48$. Under the fair-coin hypothesis,

$$
P(X\ge48\mid H_0)
=\sum_{x=48}^{50}\binom{50}{x}(0.5)^{50}
\approx1.13\times10^{-12}.
$$

::: fragment
The observed result is extremely unlikely under $H_0$.
:::

::: fragment
Therefore, we **reject the null hypothesis** that the coin is fair.
:::

::: fragment
This is the basic logic of a hypothesis test:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{assumption}
&\longrightarrow \text{reference distribution}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{tail probability}
\longrightarrow \text{decision}.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: notes
Say: “The observed result lies in an extremely unlikely tail of the
reference distribution, so the data give strong evidence against our
original assumption.”

Emphasize that a low-probability event is not impossible. A hypothesis test
uses the size of that probability to decide whether the original
assumption is still credible. The displayed probability is a one-sided
tail probability; a two-sided test would also count outcomes with at most
two heads.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed example using the Binomial distribution.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## An OLS $t$-test asks whether the slope is zero

::: columns
::: {.column width="44%"}
Test whether the population slope is zero:

$$
H_0:\beta_1=0,
\qquad
H_1:\beta_1\ne0.
$$

Statistic:

$$
t=\frac{\widehat\beta_1-0}
{SE(\widehat\beta_1)}.
$$

$SE(\widehat\beta_1)$ measures the uncertainty of $\widehat\beta_1$.

::: fragment
Large $|t|$ gives evidence against $H_0$.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-ols-t-test
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| out-width: "100%"
df_t <- 20
critical_t <- qt(0.975, df = df_t)
t_grid <- seq(-4.2, 4.2, length.out = 600)
t_density <- dt(t_grid, df = df_t)
plot(t_grid, t_density, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#2E86C1",
     xlab = "t statistic", ylab = "Density", yaxt = "n",
     main = "Two-sided 5% test", bty = "n")
left <- t_grid <= -critical_t
right <- t_grid >= critical_t
polygon(c(t_grid[left], rev(t_grid[left])),
        c(t_density[left], rep(0, sum(left))),
        col = adjustcolor("#C0392B", 0.55), border = NA)
polygon(c(t_grid[right], rev(t_grid[right])),
        c(t_density[right], rep(0, sum(right))),
        col = adjustcolor("#C0392B", 0.55), border = NA)
abline(v = c(-critical_t, critical_t), lty = 2, col = "#555555")
text(c(-3.0, 3.0), c(0.035, 0.035), c("2.5%", "2.5%"),
     col = "#9B2C2C", font = 2)
text(0, 0.08, "Do not reject", col = "#444444")
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Say: “The null hypothesis says that the population slope is zero. The
$t$-statistic measures how many standard errors the estimated slope is
from zero. Under the null hypothesis, values near zero are common. Values
far into either tail are unusual.”

The graph shows the rejection regions for an illustrative two-sided 5%
test with 20 degrees of freedom. The $p$-value is the probability, under
$H_0$, of obtaining a $t$-statistic at least as far from zero as the one we
observed.

\[Sources\] - Instructor-developed explanation and R figure based on the
Student $t$ distribution.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Any questions? {.center}

::: notes
Ask students whether they would like to revisit a probability distribution,
the OLS derivation, the coin example, or the OLS $t$-test.
:::
